questions.stem: Which of the following highest peaks is generally considered the highest point of the Western Ghats (and South India overall)?

options.option_text: Doddabetta (Tamil Nadu)
Anaimudi (Kerala)
Guru Shikhar (Rajasthan)
Kalsubai (Maharashtra)

questions.explanation: Anaimudi (2,695 metres), located in the Anaimalai Hills of Kerala, is the highest peak in the Western Ghats as well as the highest point in India south of the Himalayas. Doddabetta is the highest in the Nilgiris.

questions.stem: The Western Ghats are known locally by different names in different states. In Maharashtra, what is the traditional regional name for the Western Ghats?

options.option_text: Nilgiri Mountains
Cardamom Mountains
Sahyadri Mountains
Aravalli Mountains

questions.explanation: In Maharashtra and parts of Karnataka, the continuous chain of the Western Ghats is locally referred to as the Sahyadri mountains. The Nilgiris are further south where the Eastern and Western Ghats meet.

questions.stem: Which important mountain pass in the Western Ghats connects the city of Mumbai to Pune, serving as a critical rail and road link?

options.option_text: Thal Ghat
Pal Ghat
Shencottah Gap
Bhor Ghat

questions.explanation: Bhor Ghat connects Mumbai to Pune. Thal Ghat (or Kasara Ghat) connects Mumbai to Nashik. Pal Ghat (Palakkad Gap) is much further south, connecting Kerala (Palakkad) to Tamil Nadu (Coimbatore).

questions.stem: The major peninsular rivers Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri all originate from the Western Ghats. From which specific location does the Godavari river originate?

options.option_text: Trimbakeshwar (Maharashtra)
Mahabaleshwar (Maharashtra)
Talakaveri (Karnataka)
Amarkantak (Madhya Pradesh)

questions.explanation: The Godavari originates at Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra. The Krishna originates near Mahabaleshwar, the Kaveri at Talakaveri, and the Narmada/Son rivers originate at Amarkantak.

questions.stem: The Western Ghats block the moisture-laden southwest monsoon winds, causing heavy rainfall on their western slopes. What is this specific type of rainfall called?

options.option_text: Convectional rainfall
Cyclonic rainfall
Orographic rainfall
Frontal rainfall

questions.explanation: Orographic (relief) rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier (like the Western Ghats). It cools, condenses, and causes heavy rain on the windward side, leaving a 'rain shadow' on the leeward side.

questions.stem: Which of the following uniquely structural characteristics differentiates the Western Ghats from the typical fold mountains like the Himalayas?

options.option_text: They were formed exclusively by highly explosive massive volcanic eruptions in the recent Cenozoic era.
They are not true fold mountains, but rather the faulted edge of the down-faulted Deccan plateau block.
They are composed entirely of soft sedimentary limestone rocks created by ancient retreating seas.
They are entirely the result of the Indian plate violently colliding directly with the Eurasian plate.

questions.explanation: Unlike the Himalayas (which are true fold mountains created by tectonic collision), the Western Ghats are a 'fault scarp'. They were formed by the faulting and subsiding of the Arabian Sea flank of the peninsular landmass during the breakup of Gondwana.

questions.stem: In 2011, a high-level panel recommended declaring the entire Western Ghats as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA). Who chaired this famous committee?

options.option_text: K. Kasturirangan
M. S. Swaminathan
Vandana Shiva
Madhav Gadgil

questions.explanation: The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (WGEEP) was chaired by ecologist Madhav Gadgil. It recommended stringent protections. A later committee, chaired by K. Kasturirangan, watered down these recommendations to balance development and conservation.

questions.stem: The Western Ghats World Heritage property, inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as a serial site, spreads across how many Indian states?

options.option_text: Three states: Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu only
Five states: Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu
Four states: Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Goa
Six states: including all states along the Sahyadri range

questions.explanation: B is correct because the UNESCO Western Ghats WHS (2012) comprises 39 serial sites spanning Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu — five states in total. Option C (four states) is the most common wrong answer because Goa's contribution is often underestimated, yet the Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary and Mollem NP in Goa are included.

questions.stem: The 'Shola' ecosystem, a hallmark of the higher Western Ghats, is best described as which type of vegetation formation?

options.option_text: Dense tropical evergreen forest in low-lying coastal valleys
Montane forest patches nestled in sheltered high-altitude hollows
Semi-arid thorn scrub found on the rain-shadow leeward slopes
Riparian gallery forest fringing major rivers and streams below

questions.explanation: B is correct because Shola forests are dense, stunted montane forests that occupy sheltered depressions and valley bottoms above roughly 1,500 m in the Western Ghats, interspersed with rolling grasslands on exposed ridges — together forming the distinctive shola-grassland mosaic. Option A is wrong because Sholas are high-altitude formations, not coastal lowland forests.

questions.stem: Silent Valley National Park, which became a landmark of India's environmental movement due to opposition to a hydroelectric project on the Kunthipuzha river, is situated in which district and state?

options.option_text: Kodagu district, Karnataka — in the biodiverse Coorg region
Palakkad district, Kerala — within the Nilgiri hills zone
Nilgiris district, Tamil Nadu — near the Ooty hill station
Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka — on the coastal foothills

questions.explanation: B is correct because Silent Valley NP lies in Palakkad district, Kerala, protecting one of the last undisturbed stretches of tropical rainforest in the Western Ghats. Option C (Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu) is the most tempting error because the park falls within the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, leading candidates to incorrectly place it in Tamil Nadu.

questions.stem: The lion-tailed macaque (Macaca silenus), an Endangered primate endemic to the Western Ghats, is most distinctively identified by which physical characteristic?

options.option_text: Bright red facial patch contrasting with dense brownish-grey fur
Prominent silver-white mane radiating outward around its black face
Unusually long prehensile tail that exceeds its entire body length
Striking albino-white fur covering the upper body and shoulders

questions.explanation: B is correct because the lion-tailed macaque earns its name from the silver-white mane framing its black face and the tufted tip of its tail — resembling a lion's mane. Option A describes features closer to the bonnet macaque, which also inhabits the Western Ghats and is often confused with the lion-tailed macaque in exam stems.

questions.stem: Which biosphere reserve, spanning the tri-junction of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka within the Western Ghats, was designated as India's first biosphere reserve?

options.option_text: Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve, designated in 2001
Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, first designated in 1986
Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, designated in 1989
Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, designated in 1988

questions.explanation: B is correct because the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986) was India's first biosphere reserve under the UNESCO Man and Biosphere Programme; it was later included in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 2000. Option D (Nanda Devi, 1988) is the most common wrong answer because it is early, well-known, and also a UNESCO site, but it came two years after Nilgiri.

questions.stem: According to Conservation International's global biodiversity hotspot framework, the Western Ghats ecological region is jointly classified under a single hotspot along with which other landmass?

options.option_text: The Indo-Burma biogeographic region of mainland Southeast Asia
Sri Lanka, forming the 'Western Ghats and Sri Lanka' hotspot
The Eastern Ghats and the interior Deccan Plateau combined
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands chain in the Bay of Bengal

questions.explanation: B is correct because Conservation International designates 'Western Ghats and Sri Lanka' as one of 36 global biodiversity hotspots, reflecting their shared Gondwanan geological origin and highly similar endemic flora-fauna assemblages. Option A is the most tempting distractor because Indo-Burma is also a separate Asian hotspot that candidates frequently conflate with South Asian ecology.

questions.stem: The Kasturirangan Committee, constituted after the Gadgil panel's recommendations faced stiff opposition, submitted its Western Ghats report in 2013. What proportion of the Western Ghats did it recommend designating as Ecologically Sensitive Area?

options.option_text: Approximately 64%, retaining the full Gadgil panel recommendation
Approximately 37%, a sharply reduced area from the Gadgil report
Approximately 52%, a midpoint compromise between both panels
Approximately 22%, limited only to core protected area networks

questions.explanation: B is correct because the Kasturirangan Committee recommended ~37% (about 59,940 sq km) of the Western Ghats as ESA, far less than the Gadgil panel's ~64%, to balance conservation with livelihood and development needs of local communities. Option A (64%) is the Gadgil panel's figure — the single most common mix-up in this pair of committees, as candidates remember one number but misattribute it.
